chunks: "An eye diagram is an overlay of every bit of a data stream, folded onto a single bit period, so that all the transitions and levels are drawn on top of each other.
You make it on a scope by triggering from the clock, or a recovered clock, and displaying many bits with persistence.
The result looks like an eye: the open area in the middle is where the receiver can sample the data and get the right answer. What it represents is the margin of the link.
The vertical opening, the eye height, shows how much voltage separates a 1 from a 0 at the sampling point after ISI and noise.
The horizontal opening, eye width, shows how much time you have around the sampling instant, which is the unit interval minus jitter.
The crossing points show timing and duty cycle, and the thickness of the traces tells you about noise and jitter.
It's useful because a single picture combines all the impairments: loss and reflections show up as ISI, closing the eye from above and below; jitter blurs the crossings; noise thickens the rails.
A wide open, clean eye means low error rate; a closed eye means the receiver will make errors. And you compare it to a mask for compliance."
